thread.title: Market Extra: FAANG short sellers made nearly $1 billion in Monday’s Facebook-led plummet

title: Market Extra: FAANG short sellers made nearly $1 billion in Monday’s Facebook-led plummet
text:
Published: Mar 20, 2018 11:42 a.m. ET Share 
The strategy has been a loser over the longer term, however Getty Images Ryan Vlastelica Markets reporter 
Investors who have been betting against some of the U.S. stock market’s most popular internet and technology companies have gotten killed over the past year, a period over which equities enjoyed massive gains, but such traders racked up huge returns on Monday. 
The so-called FAANG group of stocks collapsed in Monday’s trading, led by Facebook Inc. FB, -4.88% which suffered its biggest one-day drop in nearly four years amid an uproar over how it has handled user data. The losses spread to the other FAANG names—an acronym that refers to the group of Facebook, Amazon AMZN, +2.01% Apple AAPL, +0.27% Netflix NFLX, +1.04% and Alphabet GOOGL, -0.52% the parent company of Google. 
“The reason Facebook’s selloff spread yesterday was, all these tech companies are collecting and using data. If there’s an issue here, could there be another issue elsewhere?” said Shawn Cruz, senior markets specialist at TD Ameritrade. 
That uncertainty resulted in an one-day bonanza for FAANG short sellers, who have otherwise been struggling against a group of stocks that have basically gone straight up. 
Short sellers bet against securities, making money if the price falls instead of rises. 
On Monday, when all the FAANG stocks accrued heavy losses, short sellers of the group made $980 million, according to Ihor Dusaniwsky, a managing director at research firm S3 Partners. With the day’s move, they made “back an eighth of their year-to-date losses in just one day,” he wrote in a report. 
The FAANG stocks have shown some signs of wobbling over the past several weeks, as investors sold stocks that have amid broader concerns that inflation could return to the economy, which may force the Federal Reserve to be more aggressive in raising interest rates. Such an environment is seen as less favorable to risk assets like stocks, and the FAANG group, given their massive gains over the past 12 months, could be especially vulnerable to any broader pullback. 
“Shorting FAANG stocks has been a profitable play recently, with short sellers up $1.59 billion, or 4.1%, since Monday, March 12th,” Dusaniwsky said, though he noted that “even with their recent windfall profits, FAANG shorts are still down $5.15 billion in year-to-date mark-to-market losses.” 
While Facebook turned negative for 2018 in Monday’s decline, the other FAANG stocks remain positive, in some cases standing as some of the market’s best year-to-date performers. Amazon is up 32% in 2018, and it has climbed more than 80% over the past 12 months. Apple is up 4.1% year-to-date, and 25% over the past year, while Alphabet has gained 4.3% in 2018 and 27% over the past 12 months. Netflix has been the belle of the ball, jumping more than 66% in 2018, and more than doubling over the past year. The overall S&P 500 is up 1.8% this year, and up 14.6% over the past 12 months. 
According to BofA Merrill Lynch’s March fund manager survey, the FAANG stocks—along with a trio of large Chinese tech companies—are seen as the market’s most crowded trade, with 38% of respondents taking this view. Because of that, more investors are taking the opposite side of the bet; according to Dusaniwsky’s analysis, short exposure to the FAANG stocks has increased by a third in 2018. Of the five stocks, however, Facebook had the smallest increase in short interest, up $664 million. Apple had $3.7 billion in new short exposure. Courtesy S3 Partners
